newsitem.title: UK: UK's IOD advises modest fiscal tightening.
newsitem.headline: UK's IOD advises modest fiscal tightening.

text.p: Britain's forthcoming budget should tighten fiscal policy by around 2.5 billion stg to reduce the public sector deficit, the Institute of Directors (IOD) said on Monday.

The economy may be growing well, fuelled by strong consumer demand, but this is not enough to justify a significant increase in taxation by new Chancellor of the Exchequer (finance minister) Gordon Brown, the IOD said.

"The Chancellor should resist a large increase in taxes as this would undermine his chances of controlling public sector spending in the future," the IOD said in its "recommendations for the summer budget".
No date has yet been set for the budget but Labour has pledged to hold one within two months of taking office. It ousted the 18-year old Conservative administration on May 1.
The institute recommended a fiscal tightening of about 1/4 to 1/2 percent of GDP -- equivalent to around 2.5 billion pounds.
Britain began the 1997 (April-March) financial year on a sound note, posting a public sector surplus of 36 million pounds.

But analysts attributed this to receipts from the sale of public assets and said the overall deficit -- 23.1 billion pounds in the 1996/7 financial year -- was too large given the long period of sustained growth in the economy.
Though it would like to see public sector spending cut, the institute recognised that any tightening would have to come through tax increases given the government's spending commitments.
It highlighted the phasing out of mortgage interest relief at source (MIRAS) as the least damaging option.

"There is a case for modest fiscal tightening to improve the public sector accounts. If, as seems possible, this has to be in the form of tax increases, the phased abolition of MIRAS is the least worst option," said Tim Melville-Ross, the IOD's director general.

The IOD also criticised the government's proposed windfall tax on privatised utilities as "inappropriate" and said it should be limited to the lowest possible level. But it did support the "welfare-to-work" proposals to reduce unemployment, though said they were over ambitious.

The government should maintain the existing corporation tax system, and tax credits on dividend payments, the IOD said, while priority should be given to increasing income tax personal allowances rather than to introducing a new lower tax band.

And if Brown had thought of tightening the public accounts by restricting the rate of tax relief on pension contributions, he should remember that this would reduce the incentive to make proper pension provisions, the report said.
